procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a lower court in Calcutta since the High Court set aside an order of acquittal.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of acquittal of the appellants (Puranmall Jain, Girdhari Lal, and Bhagwandeo Tewari) under s. 23(1A) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (VII of 1947).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Calcutta High Court (A. K. Das and K. K. Mitra, JJ.) set aside the order of acquittal and convicted the appellants.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (Puranmall Jain, Girdhari Lal, and Bhagwandeo Tewari) appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the judgment of the Calcutta High Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal of Puranmall Jain and acquitted him. The appeals of Girdhari Lal and Bhagwandeo Tewari were dismissed. A review petition was subsequently filed, but the outcome of that petition is not detailed in this excerpt.

decision.appeal_result: In the result the appeal of Puranmall Jain is allowed. The appeals of Girdhari Lal and Bhagwandeo Tewari are dismissed. The review petition is partly allowed and the judgment of this Court in Criminal Appeal No. 211 of 1969 modified.
decision.conviction_status: Puranmall Jain is acquitted of the charge.
decision.sentence_status: The sentence of six months' rigorous imprisonment imposed on Girdharilal is set aside. The sentence of fine of Rs. 2,000/- shall, however, stand.
directions: His bail bond shall stand cancelled.

issue.issue_text: Whether the case was fit for review because the attention of the court was not drawn specifically to sub-s. 23C(2) and the light it throws on the interpretation of sub-s.(1).

facts: After the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal, Girdharilal Gupta filed a review petition.
The basis for the review was that his counsel had failed to bring section 23C(2) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act to the court's attention during the original hearing.
The petitioner argued that this section had a "vital bearing" on the interpretation of section 23C(1), under which he was convicted.
The State argued against the review, claiming it was not a fit case for review and was merely a case of "mistaken judgment."
law: A review petition can be considered if a vital legal provision that affects the interpretation of another was not brought to the court's attention during the initial arguments.
application: The Supreme Court explicitly rejected the State's argument that the case was not fit for review.
The Court agreed with the petitioner that its attention had not been specifically drawn to s. 23C(2) and the "light it throws on the interpretation of sub-s. (1)."
The Court found this omission to be a sufficient reason to re-open the original judgment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the case was fit for review because the failure to consider section 23C(2) was a significant omission that affected the correct interpretation of section 23C(1). The court rejected the State's argument to the contrary and proceeded to re-examine the case, ultimately allowing the review petition "partly" and modifying the petitioner's sentence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the evidence of an investigating officer who conducts a search cannot be relied on unless it is corroborated.

facts: The defense counsel argued that the evidence of an investigating officer who conducts a search cannot be relied upon unless it is corroborated by other evidence.
law: The Court stated that this is a "novel proposition" with no legal principle or authority to support it.
The Court held that there is no general rule requiring an investigating officer's testimony about a search to be corroborated.
The Court clarified that the need for corroboration "all depends on the facts in each case."
application: The Court noted that, even if corroboration were required, it existed in this specific case.
The corroborating evidence included the testimony of a witness, P.W. 8, who signed the search document.
Further corroboration was found in the account books themselves, as the entries in them tallied with the slips found during the search.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, finding no legal basis for a mandatory corroboration rule and also noting that, in any event, sufficient corroborating evidence was present in this case.

issue.issue_text: Whether account slips discovered during a search could not be taken into consideration because they were not evidence.

facts: Account slips were discovered during a search of the premises.
The defense counsel argued that these slips could not be taken into consideration because they were not evidence.
application: The Court stated it was unable to appreciate the argument that the slips were not evidence.
The Court reasoned that the slips were part of the items discovered during the search.
Furthermore, the Court noted that the entries on the slips were carried into the account books and tallied with them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that there was 'no substance' to it. The Court concluded that because the slips were discovered during the search and their entries corresponded with the account books, there was no reason why they could not be looked at and taken into consideration as evidence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The mere fact that an accused person is a partner or director of a company is insufficient to make them criminally liable for offenses committed by the company; it must be established that they were in charge of the conduct of the business. A person who states they alone look after the affairs of the firm is considered to be in charge of the business within the meaning of the law. Furthermore, there is no principle that an investigating officer's evidence cannot be relied upon unless it is corroborated.
obiter: When imposing a sentence for a vicarious liability offense, a court might take notice that a person is being vicariously punished and may choose not to impose a sentence of imprisonment if it is possible the contravention took place without their knowledge or due diligence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court differentiates liability based on a partner's active role in the business. A partner who admits to being in charge of the firm's affairs is liable for contraventions unless they can prove the offense occurred without their knowledge or that they exercised due diligence to prevent it. Conversely, a partner against whom the prosecution fails to prove active participation in the business must be given the benefit of the doubt and acquitted. The court also holds that the evidence of an investigating officer is not inherently unreliable and does not require corroboration, and that a failure to consider a relevant statutory subsection is a valid ground for review.
legal_tests_applied: A person is liable for a company's offense if they are in charge of the conduct of the business, unless they can meet the burden of proof under the statutory proviso that "the contravention took place without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent such contravention."

The mere fact that an accused person is a partner or director of a company is not sufficient to make them criminally liable for offenses committed by the company; other ingredients establishing their role must be proven.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant Girdhari Lal himself stated that he alone looked after the affairs of the firm, which the court interpreted as an admission that he was in charge of the business of the firm within the meaning of the section.

The appellant Girdhari Lal failed to prove that the contravention took place without his knowledge or that he exercised due diligence to prevent it, as required by the statutory proviso to escape liability.
The court rejected the argument that the evidence of the investigating officer required corroboration, stating it was impressed by his evidence and saw no reason not to rely on it.
The court refused to presume that the investigating officer would fabricate evidence like account slips to falsely implicate the appellants.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution successfully established that appellant Girdhari Lal was in charge of the business through his own admission under s. 342, Cr.P.C.
The prosecution was not required to provide corroboration for the investigating officer's testimony, as the court found the officer's evidence credible on its own.
The prosecution was unable to lead any reliable evidence to prove that appellant Puranmall Jain took any active part in the conduct of the business of the firm, leading to his acquittal.
policy_considerations: When a person is being vicariously punished for an offense, and it is possible the contravention occurred without their knowledge or due to a lack of diligence (such as when they were abroad), a sentence of imprisonment may not be appropriate, and a fine may better meet the ends of justice.
